title: jnana: the Brahma Sutras 1.1–1.4 with Shankara

segments.voice: Last week ended on the first sutra: now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman. Jnana began as a hunger. A new week, and the second sutra says where to look.

Ask a good math teacher for the answer, and she slides the problem back across the desk. Try it again. Bhrigu gets the same treatment, and he's asking about everything. He walks up to his father, Varuna. Sir, teach me Brahman. His father doesn't define it. He gives a riddle. That from which these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they go back: try to know that. That is Brahman. So Bhrigu goes off and practices austerity, and he comes back sure he has it. Brahman is food. His father sends him away again.
screen: `THE PROBLEM, SLID BACK.` → `SIR, TEACH ME BRAHMAN.` → `BRAHMAN IS FOOD? GO AGAIN.`

segments.voice: That story is in the Taittiriya Upanishad, and Shankara reads the second sutra through it. The sutra is short: janmady asya yatah. In paraphrase: that from which the birth and the rest of this world come. The rest, Shankara explains, means its staying in being and its coming to an end. So Brahman is pointed out the way Varuna pointed it out: as the source, the support and the resting place of everything. Notice it's pointing, not picturing. The sutra doesn't say what Brahman looks like. It says where to look. Shankara adds a careful point. Isn't this just an argument, reasoning from a world to its cause? No, he says. The sutra gathers the Upanishad's own words. Reasoning helps when it agrees with them, but the knowing rests on the texts, and finally on direct realization. Which is why Varuna won't just say it. A pointed-to thing has to be seen by the one looking. Bhrigu goes again, and comes back with breath. Then mind. Then understanding. Each time, again. At last he sees Brahman as bliss, ananda. Jnana, in this story, isn't handed over at the door. It's return after return, each answer peeled back until the source shows itself.
screen: `THE SOURCE, SUPPORT AND RESTING PLACE.` · `POINTING, NOT PICTURING.` · `NOT ARGUMENT ALONE.` · then, large: `FOOD, BREATH, MIND, UNDERSTANDING, BLISS.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and walk slowly across the room and back. On the way out, notice your feet; on the way back, notice the breath; then sit, and notice what has been noticing all along. If walking isn't easy right now, make the same trip with your attention, from feet to breath to the one who's aware.
Jnana: knowledge that frees. In Bhrigu's story, it's reached by looking again and again, each answer peeled back.

howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, the Bhrigu story is often taught alongside the second sutra, and some teachers guide students to look past body, breath and mind toward the self that knows them.
